title: The Car Keys
summary: Ask your father to stop driving.
whoElse: Alan, your dad, 81, who has driven since he was seventeen and has just scraped the wing mirror off on the gatepost.
phrases: Can I talk to you about something, and can you not bite my head off?
I've been putting this off for weeks, if I'm honest.
Mum mentioned the wing mirror.
Nobody's taking anything off you.
I'm not asking you to give it up tomorrow.
Could we start with no motorways, and nothing after dark?
What would you be saying to me, if it was the other way round?
Would you rather a doctor said it than me?
Where would that leave you, day to day?
I'd rather have this row now than the other conversation later.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'Car Trouble', which is a customer explaining a fault to a mechanic — a transactional stranger conversation about a machine. This is a son taking his father's independence away, with forty years of history in the room.

title: Your Mother's Advice
summary: Ask your mother to stop giving you advice.
whoElse: Sylvia, your mum, who has opinions about your job, your flat, your cooking and the way you're raising your son, and shares all of them.
phrases: Can I say something, and you're probably not going to like it?
I know you only do it because you care.
You've done it about four times since I got here, and I've counted, which probably tells you something.
I wasn't asking, I was just telling you what's going on.
Could you just listen for a bit, without fixing it?
When I want your opinion, I promise I'll ask for it.
Honestly, 'that sounds hard' would do. That's all I'm after.
It makes me tell you less, and I don't want that.
I'd rather tell you things than start editing what I say.
Nothing's changed — I'm not having a go at you.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Screen-Time Talk', which asks someone you love to put a phone down — a habit at the dinner table. This is a lifelong power relationship: a grown adult asking their parent to stop parenting them, where the other person genuinely believes they're helping.

title: The Sibling Who Never Comes
summary: Ask your brother to share looking after Mum.
whoElse: Dan, your younger brother, two hours away, who rings your mum on Sundays and thinks that's the same thing.
phrases: I'm not ringing for a row, before you start.
When did you actually last go round?
It's every weekend, Dan. Every single one.
I'm not keeping score — well, I am, a bit, and that's the problem.
I know you're two hours away, I do know that.
Could you do one weekend in three? That's all I'm after.
Even taking the appointments off me would help.
Tell me what you can actually commit to — not what you'd like to do.
Don't say yes now just to get me off the phone.
I'd rather sort this out now than resent you in ten years.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Difficult Conversation' (giving a colleague hard feedback), which has a workplace's structure behind it — deadlines, a manager, an exit. Here there is no authority, no leaving, and the person you're negotiating with is the only other person on earth with your childhood.

title: Telling Mum
summary: Tell your mother your marriage has ended.
whoElse: Your mum, who adores your husband, has his photo in the hall, and has been asking when you're all coming for lunch.
phrases: Sit down a minute — nothing's happened to the kids.
I've got something to tell you and there's no gentle way into it.
Sam and I have separated. It's done — it's not a wobble.
It's been coming for about two years, to be honest.
I didn't tell you because I knew you'd worry, and here we are.
I know it's not what you wanted for me.
I'm alright. Not brilliant, but alright.
Please don't say anything about him — I'll only end up defending him.
Could you not ring Auntie Jean about it yet?
You don't have to say anything clever. Just be normal with me.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'Bad News', where you turn up for a grieving friend — you are the supporter, and the news is theirs. Here the news is yours, you're delivering it, and you have to manage the listener's disappointment in you while you're the one falling apart.

title: The Family Group Chat
summary: Ask your uncle to stop scaring your mum.
whoElse: Uncle Ray, your mum's brother, who forwards frightening videos and health scares into the family chat forty times a week.
phrases: I thought I'd ring rather than put this in the chat.
It's mainly the videos, to be honest.
Mum takes that stuff seriously — she doesn't know it's nonsense.
She rang me at eleven at night in a right state about it.
I know you only send it because you're worried about her.
Would you send them to me instead, and I'll have a look?
I'm not asking you to leave the group, God, no.
Could we keep it to the birthdays and the photos?
You'd hate it if someone frightened your mum like that.
I'd rather say it to you than quietly mute you, which is what I nearly did.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Group Chat', which is bowing out of a friends' trip you can't afford — a money and face problem. This is asking a relative you can never leave to change what he sends, with a third person (your mother) as the actual casualty.

title: The House
summary: Divide your father's house with your sister.
whoElse: Claire, your older sister, who nursed your dad for the last three years while you rang on Sundays, and who is now standing in his kitchen with you.
phrases: Shall we try and do this ourselves, before the solicitors get into it?
Can we get the money bit out of the way first, and then do the rest?
You did far more for him than I did. I do know that.
I'm not going to pretend I don't need the money, because I do.
Neither of us can afford to buy the other out, can we?
Could we get it valued by someone neither of us knows?
What would you want if the money wasn't in it at all?
Nothing goes to the tip until we've both been through it.
Shall we write down what we've agreed, just so neither of us misremembers?
Whatever happens, I'm not falling out with you over a kitchen.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Money You Lent' — a friend, a clean sum, one person owing another. This is two people who both have a claim, no debt, no villain, and a dead parent between them; the negotiation is about fairness and guilt rather than repayment.

title: Dad's New Partner
summary: Tell your dad you're struggling with his girlfriend.
whoElse: Your dad, widowed eighteen months, who has met Marion, is visibly happier than he's been in years, and keeps asking if you like her.
phrases: Have you got five minutes, before she gets back?
I'd rather say this badly than not say it at all.
I like her, actually. That's the honest answer.
It's just a bit quicker than I was expecting, that's all.
It's got nothing to do with her, honestly. Nothing.
I keep half expecting Mum to walk in, and that's mine to deal with, not yours.
You're allowed to be happy. I do know that.
Could you just not ask me to call her anything yet?
Give me a bit of time and I'll get there, I promise.
I don't want you creeping round your own life because of me.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Apology', which is owning a clear wrong. Here nobody has done anything wrong at all — the difficulty is admitting a feeling that isn't fair, to the person it's about, without asking him to change anything.

title: Your Brother's Debt
summary: Tell your brother you won't lend him money.
whoElse: Mark, your brother, who has borrowed from you three times, paid back once, and has just turned up on a Tuesday evening with a mug of tea and a preamble.
phrases: Before you ask — I think I know roughly what this is about.
Go on then. How much this time?
I'm going to say no, and I'd like to tell you why.
There was the van, there was the deposit, there was last March.
It's less the money now, it's that I never get a date out of you.
I'd rather lend you nothing than lend you something and end up hating you.
I'll help you with anything except this.
I'll sit down and go through the numbers with you, tonight if you want.
Don't go to Mum. Please don't go to Mum.
It's a no now and it'll still be a no on Thursday.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest are 'The Money You Lent' (chasing a friend for money already lent) and 'The Big Favour' (asking for a lot). This is the opposite move: refusing family, in advance, for the fourth time, with a parent waiting in the wings to be told.

title: Christmas at Ours
summary: Tell your mother-in-law you're not coming for Christmas.
whoElse: Barbara, your mother-in-law, who has hosted Christmas for twenty-six years and has already bought the crackers.
phrases: I wanted to ring you before it all gets booked and settled.
We're going to do Christmas at ours this year.
I know it's a change. It's the first time, isn't it.
We'd love you to come to us — genuinely, not just saying it.
The kids were in the car for five hours last year.
It's nothing anybody's done. Nothing at all.
Would Boxing Day work instead? We'd come to you for the whole day.
We're not starting a rota, I promise you that.
I know how it'll look, me ringing and not Ian.
Say what you actually think — I'd far rather hear it now than in January.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'A Wedding Invitation', where you decline an event you were invited to — a one-off, and the host has other guests. This is dismantling a tradition the other person built her year around, with your marriage and next December both in the room.

title: Your Father's Silence
summary: Get your father to talk about his past.
whoElse: Your dad, 78, who has never once talked about the year he came over, and who answers most questions with 'ah, it was a long time ago'.
phrases: Can I ask you something you'll probably not answer?
You never talk about that time at all, do you.
I'm not after anything deep. I'd just like to know, that's all.
What was she like, before we came along?
Were you frightened? I would've been.
Go on, humour me.
You don't have to tell me the whole thing.
Take your time. I'm not going anywhere.
That's more than you've ever said about it, you know.
Can we do this again? Same chair, same terrible tea.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Comparison Trap' (listening to a friend who's already talking) and 'Back in Touch' (reconnecting after a gap). Here the other person is present, close, and simply won't speak; the whole skill is drawing something out of someone who has spent fifty years not saying it.

title: The First Date
summary: Get through a first date and be honest.
whoElse: Priya — you matched three weeks ago and this is the first time you've been in a room together.
phrases: Sorry, I'm a bit early — I always do this.
Right, shall we get a drink in before we do the whole interview bit?
How was the journey over — did you have far to come?
I'll be honest, I've not done a lot of this.
Oh, whereabouts is that?
See, that's exactly what I'd have said.
Sorry, I'm talking far too much — your turn.
I'd have to think about that one, actually.
Look, I've really enjoyed this — I'd like to do it again, if you would.
I've had a lovely evening, honestly — I'm just not sure it's a romantic thing for me.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'Working the Room' (networking small talk with a stranger). That one is about turning a contact into a professional follow-up; this one is two people deciding whether they fancy each other, and it ends in a yes or a kind no — a move networking never has to make.

title: What Are We?
summary: Ask someone where you stand after four months.
whoElse: Dan — you've been seeing each other since March and neither of you has said a word about what it is.
phrases: Can I ask you something slightly awkward?
I'm not trying to pin you down, I just want to know where I am.
We've been doing this — what, four months now?
I don't need a label today, but I'd like to know one's coming.
Are you seeing other people? It's fine either way, I'd just rather know.
I'm not seeing anyone else, and I've not wanted to.
What would you call this, if someone asked you?
I'd rather have an awkward five minutes than wonder for another month.
You don't have to answer right now — but don't leave it too long, yeah?
Right. Good. That's all I needed — pudding?
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Money You Lent' (raising the unsaid thing with someone you like). That asks for a thing back; this asks for a status, where there's no owed object to point at and the other person may genuinely not know the answer yet.

title: Saying It First
summary: Say I love you before they do.
whoElse: Ellie — seven months in, on the sofa, and she does not say it back.
phrases: I'm going to say something and you don't have to do anything with it.
I love you. There — it's out.
I'm not saying it to get it back.
Don't say it because I've said it. Honestly, I'd hate that.
Take as long as you want with it.
I've been sitting on it for weeks, if I'm honest.
Is it too soon? You can say if it is.
I'd rather have said it and been wrong about the timing.
So — are we alright?
Right, we're never speaking of this again. Put the kettle on.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Big Favour' (ask for a lot, mean it that no is fine). That protects the other person's right to refuse a request; here there is nothing being requested at all — the whole skill is saying a thing that cannot be answered on demand and then not flinching at the silence.

title: Meeting His Mum
summary: Survive Sunday lunch with your partner's mother.
whoElse: Carol — your partner's mum, who has been cooking since nine and has a lot of questions.
phrases: Thank you so much for having me — I've heard a lot about this kitchen.
Can I give you a hand with anything?
That's very kind, but I'm honestly fine with the one.
He's told me that story about six times, so I'm well briefed.
It's early days, but it's going well.
I wouldn't like to say, honestly — ask me in a year.
I'll let him answer that one.
This is genuinely lovely — is it your recipe?
I'd better let you get on.
Thank you, really — you've made it very easy.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'Talking About the Weather' (warm small talk with a neighbour). That is between equals with nothing at stake; here one person is auditioning, the questions are pointed, and half the skill is answering without answering.

title: A Row About Nothing
summary: Stop a row about the bin getting worse.
whoElse: Sam — your partner, and it started over the bin twenty minutes ago.
phrases: Hang on — are we actually arguing about the bin?
Can we start that again? I came in like a bear.
That came out worse than I meant it.
I don't think this is about the bin, is it.
You're doing the thing where you go quiet.
Alright — that's fair. That one's on me.
Can we not do this at half eleven at night?
I'm not having a go. I promise I'm not.
Say what you actually mean, and I won't get cross.
Right. Truce. Come here.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Apology' (say sorry when you were properly wrong). That is a clean, prepared apology delivered after the fact for a known offence; this is live, both people are wrong, nobody has prepared anything, and the move is stopping a thing while it is still happening.

title: Moving In
summary: Say yes to moving in, with conditions.
whoElse: Marta — she's found a two-bed and she wants an answer this week.
phrases: So — are we talking about this properly, or just talking about it?
I want to, I do. I've just got a couple of practical worries.
Can I be the boring one and talk about money?
Whose name would actually be on it?
I'd need somewhere I can shut the door, if I'm honest.
What happens to my flat — do I keep it for a bit, or is that mad?
I don't want us to find this out the hard way.
Would you be alright with a trial run — six months?
The stuff I'm nervous about is all small stuff. That's what worries me.
Go on then. Let's do it.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'Working From Home' (two of you, one table, sort out the space). That negotiates a system between people who already live together; this decides whether to live together at all, and the sticking points are the lease, the money and the exit.

title: Her Ex
summary: Tell your partner their ex is bothering you.
whoElse: Nadia — your partner, who still has coffee with Tom and didn't mention the last one.
phrases: Can I say something, and can you not make me feel mad for saying it?
It's not that I don't trust you. It's that I don't know him.
I'm not asking you to stop seeing him.
It's the not-mentioning-it that got me, more than the coffee.
I'd rather hear it from you than see it on your phone.
I know how this sounds.
I'm a bit jealous, and I'm not proud of it.
What is he to you now, honestly?
If it were the other way round, would you be fine with it?
Just tell me when you're seeing him. That's genuinely all.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Screen-Time Talk' (a gentle boundary with someone you love). That asks for a change of habit and the speaker holds the moral high ground; here the speaker is the one who might be in the wrong, and the hard part is admitting an unflattering feeling out loud without turning it into an accusation.

title: "I'm Fine"
summary: Get your partner to say what's actually wrong.
whoElse: Alex — your partner, who has been monosyllabic since Tuesday and says nothing's the matter.
phrases: You've been off all evening. What's going on?
'Fine' is doing a lot of work there.
I'd rather you told me and it was awkward.
Have I done something? Just say if I have.
I'm not going to be cross. I might be, later, but not now.
Take your time. I'm not going anywhere.
Is it me, or is it work, or is it just one of those days?
You don't have to have it all worked out to tell me.
Alright — I'll leave it. But come and find me, yeah?
I'd honestly rather a row than the silence.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Comparison Trap' (listening well to a friend who feels behind). There the friend is already talking and wants to; here the other person is actively refusing to, the speaker may be the cause, and the skill is asking twice and then knowing when to stop asking.

title: Ending It
summary: End a two-year relationship to their face.
whoElse: Leo — two years together, and he has no idea this is coming.
phrases: I need to talk to you, and it's not a good one.
I don't want to do this anymore. I'm sorry.
I've been thinking about it for a while — I know it's out of nowhere for you.
There's nobody else. I know that's the first question.
It's not going to make sense tonight, and I'm not going to pretend it will.
I'm not going to change my mind. I'd rather be honest about that than leave you hoping.
You've done nothing wrong. I know that's no use.
Ask me anything you want. I'll answer it.
I'll go to my sister's tonight — you stay here.
I did love you. That's not a thing I'm saying to be kind.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'Resigning' (leave without being talked out of it). That ends a contract with someone who has no emotional claim on you and where 'it's not you' is a lie everyone accepts; here the person will be devastated in the room, and the speaker has to hold a decision while causing visible pain.

title: Being Dumped
summary: Be dumped, and ask why.
whoElse: Rosie — she sat you down twenty minutes ago and it's already over.
phrases: Right. Okay. Give me a second.
Is this a decision or a conversation?
How long have you known?
Don't soften it. Just tell me straight.
Is there someone else? I'd rather know now than in six months.
I'm not going to beg.
Can I ask you one thing and then I'll stop?
I think I need you to leave, actually.
I'm not being cold. I just can't do this bit in front of you.
Thank you for doing it to my face.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Performance Review' (take the criticism, ask for what you want). That is bad news you can negotiate with; this is bad news that is already final, and the only moves left are finding out what you need to know and choosing how the room ends.

title: At the Dentist
summary: Tell the dentist you're frightened of the drill.
whoElse: Nadia Rahman, a dentist who has seen every kind of frightened adult.
phrases: I'll be honest with you, I've been putting this off for years.
I'm not great with dentists, I'm afraid.
It's the drill more than anything.
Could you tell me what you're doing as you go? I hate not knowing.
If I put my hand up, could we stop for a second?
It's this one at the back — it's been giving me grief when I drink anything cold.
How much are we talking, roughly?
Is that something that needs doing now, or could it wait a bit?
Am I going to feel anything?
I'd rather have it done today than sit and worry about it for a fortnight.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'At the Doctor's', which is about describing symptoms clearly to a GP. This one isn't about describing anything — the problem is the patient's own fear and the money, and the whole conversation happens with someone about to put their hands in your mouth.

title: The Embarrassing Bit
summary: Tell your doctor the thing you've been hiding.
whoElse: Dr Owen Pryce, a GP with about seven minutes and no shock left in him.
phrases: There's actually something else, while I'm here.
This is going to sound daft, but…
I'm a bit embarrassed about this, to be honest.
I've been sitting on this for a few months, if I'm honest.
I've probably left it far too long.
I did have a look online, which was a mistake.
Sorry — I'm not really sure how to say this.
Would you mind if I just showed you?
Am I wasting your time with this?
Is this the sort of thing you see a lot?
notDuplicateBecause: 'At the Doctor's' teaches a patient who wants to explain their symptom. Here the patient does not want to explain it, and the lesson is the language of getting a sentence out at all — the 'while I'm here' door-handle moment that GPs say is most of their real work.

title: The Receptionist
summary: Get an appointment when there aren't any left.
whoElse: Denise on the surgery front desk, keeper of a diary that is always full.
phrases: I know you're rushed off your feet, but I could really do with being seen.
Is there anything at all, even later in the week?
What are my options here?
I'd take a cancellation if one came up — I'm five minutes away.
Is there a waiting list I could put my name on?
Would it help if I rang back at eight tomorrow?
I don't want to make a fuss, but it's got noticeably worse since Friday.
I'm happy to see anyone — it doesn't have to be my usual doctor.
Is that something the nurse could do instead?
You've been really good about this — thanks for trying.
notDuplicateBecause: 'At the Doctor's' starts once you're already in the room. This is the conversation that decides whether you ever get in the room, and it's with a gatekeeper who can't help you but can choose to. Nearest in feel is 'At the Museum' (talking past a sold-out tour), but the stakes are health, not a ticket.

title: A Second Opinion
summary: Ask your doctor for a second opinion.
whoElse: Dr Helen Curtis, your GP for eleven years, who has been good to you.
phrases: I want to say this the right way, because I'm not unhappy with you.
I'd like to get another opinion, if that's alright.
It's nothing to do with you — I just can't quite settle with it.
I know you've explained it, and I've still got a nagging doubt.
Would you be able to refer me to someone?
Am I within my rights to ask for that?
What would you do, if it were you?
I'd rather ask now than wonder about it for a year.
Is there anything I'd be giving up by going down that route?
Thank you for not taking it personally — I do appreciate it.
notDuplicateBecause: 'At the Doctor's' ends with the patient reassured. This one is what happens when they aren't, and the difficulty is social rather than medical: questioning an expert you like and have to keep seeing. 'Making a Complaint' is the nearest, but there is no fault here and nothing to be put right.

title: What It Actually Means
summary: Make a consultant explain your diagnosis in English.
whoElse: Mr Adeyemi, a hospital consultant who talks fast and means well.
phrases: Could I stop you there? I've lost you a bit.
Sorry — what does that mean in plain English?
Can I just check I've understood: you're saying it's not cancer?
So, in normal words, what happens to me next?
I'm going to repeat it back to you, and you tell me if I've got it wrong.
Do you mind if I write this down?
Is it alright if I record this? I'll only forget half of it.
What would you be worried about, if you were me?
What's the realistic best case, and what's the worst?
Who do I ring if I think of something tomorrow?
notDuplicateBecause: 'At the Doctor's' has a couple of clarifying lines ('should I take these with food?'). Here clarifying IS the whole lesson, under fear, with a specialist rather than a GP — interrupting someone senior, repeating information back, and leaving with something you can actually tell your family.

title: Ringing 999
summary: Ring 999 for a friend who's collapsed.
whoElse: the ambulance call handler, calm on the other end, asking the same question again.
phrases: Ambulance, please.
Right — he's collapsed, he's breathing, but he's not really with it.
The address is 14 Fenton Road, flat 3 — the buzzer's broken, I'll come down.
He's fifty-two. No, nothing like this before.
Give me a second — I'm just going to check.
Yes, he's breathing. I can see his chest going.
Sorry, can you say that again? I'm not thinking straight.
Tell me what you want me to do and I'll do it.
How long are we looking at, roughly?
I'm staying on the line — I'm not going anywhere.
notDuplicateBecause: Nothing in the sixty is an emergency. 'At the Vet' has a worried owner, but there's time there and a person in front of you. This is a stranger on a phone, no politeness budget, and the language is the opposite of everything else on the site: address first, take instructions, answer the question asked.

title: Pain Nobody Believes
summary: Make a doctor take your pain seriously.
whoElse: Dr Rowan Fitch, who has skimmed your notes and thinks he knows this one.
phrases: I've been in twice about this now, so bear with me.
I know it doesn't show up on anything. It's still there.
I'm not after painkillers. I'm after knowing what it is.
On a bad day I can't get my shoes on.
It's not that I can't cope with it — it's that it's not getting better.
I have tried that, actually, for about four months.
I'd like it written in my notes that I've raised it again.
I'm not imagining it, and I think I'm being told that I am.
What would need to happen for me to get a scan?
I'm not going to keep coming back and saying the same thing — so what's the next step?
notDuplicateBecause: 'At the Doctor's' is a first visit that goes well and ends in reassurance. This is the fourth visit that hasn't, where the patient is being gently dismissed and has to push without becoming 'difficult'. Closest in register is 'At the Bank' ('with respect, I've already explained this twice') — but that's money, and someone else can fix it.

title: The First Session
summary: Say why you're there in your first session.
whoElse: Ruth Mbeki, a therapist, fifty minutes, first appointment.
phrases: I don't really know how this works, so you might have to steer me.
I'm not sure where to start, to be honest.
Nothing's happened, exactly. That's part of what's bothering me.
It's been building up for a while rather than one big thing.
I've never said this out loud before.
Sorry, give me a minute.
I'm not sure that came out right.
I suppose what I want is to stop feeling like this on Sunday nights.
Can I ask what actually happens in these sessions?
That's more than I meant to say, but I'm glad I did.
notDuplicateBecause: Nothing existing covers therapy. 'The Comparison Trap' is the nearest, but that's the listener's job with a friend — this is the speaker's job with a professional, where the usual English politeness moves ('I'm fine', 'it's nothing really') are exactly the thing you have to stop doing.

title: Not Coping
summary: Tell your oldest friend you're not okay.
whoElse: Priya, your oldest friend, who keeps asking and won't be fobbed off.
phrases: Can I tell you something, and you not do anything about it?
I've said I'm fine about four times now and I'm not.
I'm not in danger or anything — I want to say that first.
I'm just knackered in a way that sleep doesn't fix.
I keep meaning to ring you and then I don't.
I didn't want to put it on you.
I don't need advice. I just needed one person to know.
Please don't ring my mum.
If you ask me next week, ask me properly.
Sorry. I hate this bit.
notDuplicateBecause: 'The Comparison Trap' and 'Bad News' both put the student in the supporting chair — listening to someone else's trouble. This one turns the chair round: the student is the one who's struggling, and has to say so to someone who loves them, which is a completely different set of phrases.

title: Mum's Appointment
summary: Speak up when your mum won't.
whoElse: Dr Shah, and your mother, who says she's absolutely fine.
phrases: Mum, do you want to tell him, or shall I?
She's playing it down, I'm afraid.
Sorry to speak for you — stop me if I get it wrong.
Can I add something she won't say?
She's had three falls since Christmas, not one.
Would you mind speaking to her rather than me?
Mum, is that fair, or am I exaggerating?
I don't want to talk about her as if she's not here.
What should we be watching for at home?
Is there anything she could be referred for — even just to be looked at?
notDuplicateBecause: Every existing medical lesson has two people in the room. This has three, and the student is the only one telling the truth — they must contradict their own mother in front of a doctor without humiliating her. Can you give me a date rather than 'soon'?
I'd rather sort this between us than go through anybody else.
If cash flow's tight, tell me and we'll do it in two payments.
I can't start the next piece until this one's settled — that's not a threat, it's just where I am.
Who actually presses the button on payments?
Right — the 30th. I'll put that in an email and we'll say no more about it.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Money You Lent', which is a friend and a favour. This is a commercial relationship the student wants to keep — the money is owed contractually, the other person is charming rather than defensive, and the move is turning warmth into a date without losing the client.

title: The Truce
summary: Agree to work with someone you dislike.
whoElse: Stefan Bauer — a colleague you cannot stand, and with whom you've just been paired for six months.
phrases: Can we have an awkward two minutes and then never mention it again?
We're not each other's favourite, are we?
I'm not asking us to be friends.
We've got six months of this — I'd rather it wasn't horrible.
I'll be honest, I found the thing in the meeting a bit annoying.
That's fair. I probably do do that.
Can we agree to say it to each other rather than about each other?
What do you need from me to make this work?
If I'm getting on your nerves, just tell me.
Right — that's that. Shall we get on with it?
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Difficult Conversation', which is one person giving another feedback about performance. Here nobody is in the wrong and nobody is in charge — it's mutual dislike, openly named, with the modest goal of a workable six months rather than improvement or resolution.

title: Not Coping at Work
summary: Tell your manager you're struggling to cope.
whoElse: Neil Harker — your manager. Decent enough, but has never once asked how you are.
phrases: There's something I should have said about a month ago.
I'm not coping, and I'd rather say it now than fall over in front of a client.
It's not one thing. It's all of it, and I've run out of road.
I've been getting by, but I'm getting by on fumes.
I'm not asking to be let off. I'm asking for it to change.
I've stopped sleeping properly, if I'm honest with you.
I don't need an answer today.
Two weeks would make an enormous difference.
This isn't me handing my notice in.
Thanks for not making that harder than it was.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'Saying No to Your Boss', which is a tactical, cheerful triage of one extra task — the student is fine, just busy. This one is the admission underneath that: the student is not fine, the subject is health rather than scheduling, and the risk being managed is looking weak in front of the person who decides their future.

title: The Joke
summary: Tell a colleague his joke wasn't funny.
whoElse: Rob Whelan — popular, generous, everybody's mate, and he keeps doing Aisha's accent.
phrases: Have you got a sec? It's a small thing.
That thing you said about Aisha's accent — it didn't land well.
I know you didn't mean anything by it.
I laughed at the time, which is my fault as much as yours.
I'm not making a formal thing of this. I'd rather just say it.
It's the kind of thing that's funny once and then isn't.
Put it this way — would you have said it if she'd been standing there?
I'm not calling you anything. I'm telling you how it sounded.
That's all I wanted to say. Genuinely.
Don't be weird with me now, will you?
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'Taking the Credit', which is the student defending their own interest. Here the student has lost nothing and is speaking up on someone else's behalf, to a popular colleague, about something they themselves laughed at — the difficulty is having no standing and no grievance, only an objection.

title: The Scam Call
summary: Refuse a caller who says he's your bank.
whoElse: "Ryan from the fraud team" — calm, patient, knows your address, and is not who he says he is.
phrases: Sorry — before we go any further, who am I actually speaking to?
I'm not being funny, but I've no way of knowing that, have I.
I'd rather ring you back on the number on the back of my card.
How did you get this number, out of interest?
I'm not going to be reading anything out over the phone, I'm afraid.
You'll appreciate I can't just take your word for it.
If it's genuinely that urgent, it'll still be urgent in ten minutes.
No, I'm alright, thanks — I'll sort it through the app.
You're welcome to put it in writing.
Right — I'm going to hang up now. Nothing personal.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'At the Bank' (a real branch problem you want fixed). Here the whole task is the opposite: not cooperating, not being helpful, and getting off the phone while someone pleasant applies pressure.

title: The First Phone Call
summary: Ring a match before you agree to meet.
whoElse: Priya — three weeks of messaging, and neither of you has heard the other's voice.
phrases: Right — this is a bit odd, isn't it, after all that typing.
I'll be honest, I'm rubbish on the phone.
Can I ask you something slightly nosy?
Whereabouts are you, roughly? You don't have to say.
What made you say yes to this, out of interest?
I've had a couple of these that went nowhere, if I'm honest.
You're much easier to talk to than I'd built up in my head.
Shall we just do a coffee and see how we go?
Somewhere public, and I'll tell my sister where I am — I hope that's not weird.
If either of us wants to make an excuse and go after twenty minutes, that's completely fine.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'Back in Touch' (repairing an old friendship). This is a stranger you've only read, with the specific job of deciding whether to meet — and saying the safety bit out loud without making it sound like an accusation.

title: The Thing You Shared
summary: Admit your post was wrong and correct it.
whoElse: Nadia, from your street's WhatsApp group — she's checked the story you shared, and it isn't true.
phrases: Hang on — let me actually read it properly.
Where's this from originally? I never checked, did I.
God, I feel a bit daft now.
You're right, and I'm not going to argue with it.
I'll take it down now, while we're talking.
Deleting it isn't really enough, though, is it — people have seen it.
I'll put something up saying I got it wrong.
Would you rather I named you in it, or left you out of it altogether?
I should have checked before I hit share. That's the bit that bothers me.
Thanks for telling me rather than letting me carry on.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Apology' (a private betrayal, no fix available). This one has an audience and a practical job attached: agreeing what the correction says and who it names, in public, now.

title: The Comment Row
summary: Ring someone you argued with in the comments.
whoElse: Gary — your sister's husband. You've been going at each other under someone else's post for two days, and there's a barbecue on Saturday.
phrases: Look, I'm not ringing for round two.
I'd rather have this out properly than type at you.
It got a bit out of hand, didn't it.
Some of what I put was fair. The last one wasn't.
I don't think either of us was really talking to each other by the end.
Fair enough — I can see how it read.
That's not what I meant, but I can see why you took it that way.
Half of it was for the people watching, if I'm honest.
Can we just leave it there and have a beer on Saturday?
I'll delete mine if you delete yours — or leave them, I don't mind, honestly.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Collab' (disagreeing pleasantly about a film). Here the disagreement already happened, in public, in writing, and can't be unsaid — the work is cooling it down with someone you'll be sitting next to at the weekend.

title: The Group Admin
summary: Tell a group member to stop posting adverts.
whoElse: Tomasz — he's in the 300-member running group you run, and he's quietly turned it into his shop window.
phrases: Can I have a quick word about the group — wearing my admin hat?
It's not a personal thing, and I'd say the same to anyone.
The rule's the same for everybody — that's the only reason I'm ringing.
I've had three people message me about it, which is why it's landed on me.
You're welcome to post it once, and that's genuinely fine.
I know it's your livelihood — I'm not trying to make that harder.
If it carries on I'll have to start taking them down, and I'd rather not.
I don't want to remove you. That's the honest position.
Is that something you can live with?
Right — no hard feelings, I hope. See you Sunday.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Group Chat' (bowing out of a trip you can't afford). That's a member protecting themselves; this is the person holding the rule, with the power to remove someone and no wish to use it.

title: The Café Poster
summary: Ask a business to pay for your photo.
whoElse: Elena — she runs the café at the end of the road, and your photograph is on every poster in the window.
phrases: I think that might be my photo you've got on the poster.
I'm fairly sure it's mine — it's the one from that frosty morning in January.
I'm not cross about it, before you panic.
I'd have said yes if you'd asked, that's the funny thing.
It's less about the money and more about being asked.
Where else has it gone — is it just the poster, or the website as well?
Two options, really: you credit me and pay something, or it comes down.
I'd normally charge a hundred for something like that.
Could we say fifty and my name on the website?
Next time just send me a message and it's yours.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'A Photo of You' (asking a friend to take down a photo you're in). This is the reverse: you took the picture, a business is using it, and you're negotiating credit and money rather than asking for a favour.

title: The Bad Seller
summary: Get your money back from a private seller.
whoElse: Deniz — he sold you a "barely used" bike online, and you're both standing in a car park with it.
phrases: Thanks for meeting me — I'll not keep you long.
It's not what was in the advert, though, is it.
You said barely used. Have a look at the state of the chain.
I'm not accusing you of anything, but this didn't happen in three days.
What I'd like is the ninety back, and you take the bike.
I'm not after a bit off. I want to undo it.
I'd rather sort it here than start leaving reviews and messaging you every day.
Cash is fine, or a transfer — whatever's easiest for you.
I'm not going to go away on this, I'm afraid.
Right, that's it done — no hard feelings, honestly.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest are 'Making a Complaint' and 'The Delivery Gone Wrong' — both against a company, where policy and a refund process exist. Here there's no company, no policy, no comeback: just a bloke in a car park who has your money and can simply walk off.

title: The AI Mistake
summary: Tell a colleague their AI wrote something false.
whoElse: Beth — she drafted the client report with an AI, there's a figure in it that doesn't exist, and it goes out at four.
phrases: Have you got two minutes before this goes out?
Where's this figure come from, do you know?
I've had a look and I can't find it anywhere.
I think it might have made it up, to be honest.
It does that, apparently — it fills the gap in rather than saying it doesn't know.
I'm not going to say anything to anyone. I just don't want it going to the client.
Can we pull the number out and just say what we actually know?
I've done exactly the same thing, so I'm not standing here judging you.
Do you want me to go through the rest of it with you?
Nobody else needs to know — it hasn't gone anywhere yet.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest are 'The Mistake' (confessing your own error upward) and 'The Difficult Conversation' (formal feedback about a pattern). This is sideways and urgent: a peer, one specific error, minutes to fix it, and no authority to make them do anything.

title: The Frozen Interview
summary: Save a job interview when the video freezes.
whoElse: Frank — he's interviewing you for the job, and his face has just frozen mid-question.
phrases: Sorry — I think I've lost you for a second there.
Can you still hear me, or is it just me?
You went a bit robotic — would you mind saying that again?
I'll turn my camera off and see if that helps.
Shall we just do it on the phone instead? I'm happy either way.
I think it's my end, not yours.
Sorry, you go — I'm talking over you.
Where had we got to? You were asking about the Renner project.
Bear with me two seconds while I move nearer the router.
Sorry about all that — thanks for being patient with it.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest are 'The Interview' and 'A Job Interview' (content: the pitch, the weakness). This teaches nothing about selling yourself — it's the repair language for when the medium fails and you have to hold the room together while you can't see the other person.

title: The Review They Want Down
summary: Stand by a bad review you left.
whoElse: Gavin — the plumber you gave two stars, ringing you at half eight in the evening.
phrases: I wasn't expecting a call about it, I'll be honest.
I stand by what I put, but I'm happy to talk about it.
Everything in it happened. I've not exaggerated any of it.
I did try ringing you twice before I wrote anything.
I'm not going to take it down, I'm afraid.
If you refund the callout I'll add that you sorted it — I'm not going to delete it, though.
I'd rather you didn't ring me at this time of night, actually.
I've left plenty of good ones. This one just wasn't.
You're welcome to reply to it publicly — that's what the reply box is for.
I think we'll have to leave it there. Goodnight.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Honest Review' (you kindly telling an owner the truth, face to face, wanting them to do well). Here the pressure runs the other way — he's rung you, he wants it gone, and the task is refusing a man who is upset and possibly right to be.

title: The Wrong Person
summary: Tell your boss you didn't do it.
whoElse: Dan Reilly, your line manager, who's been told you leaked a client list and half believes it.
phrases: Can we go back a step? I want to be sure I've understood what I'm being accused of.
That wasn't me.
I'd rather hear it from you than get it second-hand.
Who's told you that?
I can see why it looks like that, but it wasn't me.
I'm not going to pretend I'm not annoyed.
Have a look at the file history — it'll tell you more than I can.
I'm happy to go through it with you line by line, if that helps.
What happens now?
I'd like to know you've actually got to the bottom of it, not just dropped it.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Mistake' (English at Work), where the student owns an error and manages the fallout. This is the exact opposite move: the student is innocent and has to say so without sounding defensive or making an enemy of the boss. Different language entirely — challenging the source, asking for evidence, staying employable while saying no.

title: The Car Park Scrape
summary: Own up to scraping a stranger's car.
whoElse: Maureen, who's just come back to her car with a shopping trolley and found you standing by the dent.
phrases: That'll be me, I'm afraid.
I did think about leaving a note, but I'd rather tell you myself.
It was completely my fault — I misjudged the gap.
It's only a scuff, but it's a scuff I've put there.
Shall we do it through the insurance, or would you rather I just paid for it?
Get a couple of quotes and send them to me.
Here's my number and my registration — take a photo of my licence too, if you want.
I'd rather sort it now than have you chasing me for a month.
Have a proper look before we leave it — is there anything else?
I'm really sorry. I know it's the last thing you needed today.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'Car Trouble' (Everyday Echoes), which is a customer describing a fault to a mechanic and questioning a quote. Nothing there is about fault or admission. This is a confession to a stranger with money attached and no relationship to soften it — the practical language of insurance, quotes and details, which no existing lesson touches.

title: The Lie Found Out
summary: Face a friend who caught you lying.
whoElse: Tomás, your oldest friend, who you told you were ill — and who saw the photos of you at someone else's dinner.
phrases: Yeah. You're right. I wasn't ill.
I'm not going to try and wriggle out of it.
I lied to you, and then I let it sit there for a week.
It started as a small thing and then I couldn't get out of it.
There's no good version of this — I just didn't want to say no to you.
I know sorry doesn't really cover it.
Ask me anything you like. I'll tell you straight.
You've every right to be furious.
I'd rather you shouted, honestly.
I know it'll take you a while to trust that. That's fair enough.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Apology' (Modern Life), where the student volunteers a confession about repeating something told in confidence. Here the student is caught first and has to answer questions in real time rather than deliver a prepared admission — the pressure, and the language, is reactive: no announcement, just answering.

title: Stopped by the Police
summary: Answer a police officer who's got you wrong.
whoElse: PC Ellis, who's stopped you two streets from a break-in because you match the description.
phrases: Sorry — am I being detained, or am I free to go?
Can I ask what this is about?
Of course. I've got no problem with that.
I'm happy to answer, I'd just like to know why you're asking.
I've been at work since eight — my manager can confirm that.
There's a card in my back pocket — is it alright if I reach for it?
I think you've got the wrong person, honestly.
I'm not being difficult. I'd just like to understand what's happening.
Could I take your name and number, please?
Am I going to hear anything more about this?
notDuplicateBecause: Nothing in the 60 involves authority with power over you. 'Making a Complaint' and 'At the Bank' are both the student pushing an institution; here the institution is pushing the student and the whole skill is compliance-with-clarity — knowing what to ask, when to agree, and how not to escalate. Genuinely needed by adults living abroad.

title: The Row You Started
summary: Go back to your sister after a row.
whoElse: Nadia, your sister, who you had a go at over dinner in front of everyone.
phrases: Have you got two minutes? I'm not here to carry it on.
I've been going over it, and I started it.
What I said about your job was out of order.
I was tired, but that's not really an excuse, is it?
You didn't do anything wrong — I just went for you.
I'd been sitting on it for weeks and it came out sideways.
I'm not asking you to say your bit was fine. I just wanted to do mine first.
Can we not do the thing where we don't speak for a month?
Say what you need to say. I'll shut up.
Are we alright?
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Apology' (Modern Life), which is a single clean act of wrongdoing confessed to a friend. A row is two-sided and unresolved: the student is partly wrong, partly wronged, and the move is going first anyway without demanding the other half. Family, not friendship — you can't walk away from it.

title: The Hollow Apology
summary: Tell someone their apology isn't enough.
whoElse: Greg, a colleague apologising for the third time for landing you with his work at five on a Friday.
phrases: I appreciate you saying it. I'm not sure I believe it, though.
Can I be honest with you? That's what you said last time.
The apology's fine. It's the third one, that's the problem.
I'd rather you didn't say sorry and just changed it.
What's actually going to be different this time?
Don't apologise to me — tell me what you're going to do.
I'm not trying to punish you.
Sorry, but 'it won't happen again' — what does that mean in practice?
Let's talk again in a fortnight and see where we are.
If it happens again I'll have to take it to Ruth, and I'd rather you heard that from me now.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Difficult Conversation' (English at Work), which is unprompted feedback on a pattern. Here the other person has already apologised, which is socially designed to close the conversation — the skill is declining to let it close, politely, and that's a specific and rare set of moves not taught anywhere in the 60.

title: Letting It Go
summary: Forgive an old friend after ten years.
whoElse: Alan, a friend from years back who let you take the fall at work and never once mentioned it.
phrases: I've wanted to say this for a long time and I keep not saying it.
I'm not after an apology. I've stopped waiting for one, honestly.
It did hurt me, and I'm not going to pretend it didn't.
I've carried it around for years and I'm tired of it, to be honest.
As far as I'm concerned, it's done.
That doesn't mean it was alright. It means I'm not carrying it about anymore.
I'd rather have you around than be right about it.
You don't have to say anything. Honestly.
Can we just start from here?
I've said my piece. Shall we get a coffee?
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'Back in Touch' (Modern Life), which is warm reconnection after drift with nothing actually wrong between them. This one has a real injury in the middle of it and the student is choosing to release it without getting the apology — the opposite of every other lesson in the group, which are all about extracting or delivering accountability.

title: The Missing Money
summary: Ask your flatmate about money that's gone.
whoElse: Dee, your flatmate of two years, and the bills jar in the kitchen that's sixty quid light.
phrases: This is going to sound worse than I mean it, so bear with me.
I'm not accusing you of anything — I want to be really clear about that.
There was about eighty quid in the jar and now there's twenty.
Have you moved it, or borrowed it, or…?
If you've taken it, just say. It genuinely isn't the end of the world.
I'd rather ask you than sit here wondering.
I've looked everywhere else, which is why I'm asking.
Is everything alright? You'd tell me if you were short.
Then I've got it wrong, and I'm sorry for asking.
Can we put it in an account instead, so neither of us has to think about it?
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Money You Lent' (Modern Life), where the debt is agreed and the only question is when it's paid. Here nothing is agreed and the student may be entirely wrong — the skill is raising a suspicion you can't prove, and leaving the other person a way out. Different risk: you can't unsay it.

title: The Borrowed Thing
summary: Tell a friend you broke her camera.
whoElse: Ines, who lent you her father's camera lens for the weekend, and you've cracked it.
phrases: I've got to tell you something and you're not going to like it.
Your lens — I've cracked it.
It was in my bag and I put the bag down too hard. That's it, that's all it was.
I'm not going to make it sound better than it is.
I'll pay for it. That's not a question.
Don't say that — I'd rather you let me sort it.
Let me find out what a new one costs and I'll transfer it tonight.
If they can repair it, I'll cover that; if not, I'll replace it.
I know it was your dad's, which makes it worse.
I should have told you on Sunday and I didn't, and that's the bit I feel worst about.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is 'The Mistake' (English at Work), which is a professional error reported upward where the currency is damage control and hierarchy. This is a friend, an object with sentimental value, and money that the friend will refuse to take — the negotiation of insisting on paying while someone waves you away is its own conversation, taught nowhere in the 60.

title: At the Wake
summary: Speak to a widow you barely know.
whoElse: Bernadette, David's widow — she is shaking two hundred hands today, and yours is one of them.
phrases: I'm so sorry. I don't really know what else to say.
You won't remember me — I worked with David years ago.
I don't want to keep you, there's a queue behind me.
He talked about you constantly, you know.
I only knew him at work, but he was very good to me when I started.
Is there anything at all you need doing today?
I won't ask how you are — it's a daft question today.
Would it be alright if I rang you in a few weeks, when everyone's gone home?
Take your time, honestly, there's no rush.
It was a lovely service. He'd have hated the fuss.
notDuplicateBecause: Closest is Bad News, but that is a private, unlimited, sitting-on-the-sofa conversation with a close friend where you can say nothing at all. This is ninety seconds in a receiving line with someone you hardly know, in public, with people behind you — the constraint is the whole lesson.

title: The Speech Check
summary: Read your speech to someone who'll cut it.
whoElse: Priya, the bride's sister — she knows which jokes will land and which will end a marriage.
phrases: Can I read you something? Be brutal.
I'd rather you told me now than the whole room found out.
Is that too much, do you think?
Too soon for that one?
Right, that's going. No argument.
I'm not precious about it — cut whatever you want.
Does that land, or is it just funny to me?
The bit I'm not sure about is the ex.
How long is too long, realistically?
Fine — I'll keep the dog story and lose the rest.
notDuplicateBecause: A Leaving Party teaches the toast itself; The Presentation teaches surviving Q&A after you've spoken. This is the conversation the night before — asking someone to take a knife to your words and not defending them. The skill is receiving cuts, not delivering lines.

title: The New Baby
summary: Visit a new mum and actually be useful.
whoElse: Cara, three weeks in — she's had eleven visitors and nobody has washed a cup.
phrases: I'm not staying, I've just come to drop this off.
Shall I put the kettle on? Sit down.
Where do the clean ones live?
Never mind her, how are you?
You don't have to entertain me, honestly.
Say the word and I'll go.
Has anyone actually asked you that yet?
You look shattered. Go and lie down, I'll sit with her.
I'll come Tuesday and do the same, if that's any use.
Don't tidy up on my account.
notDuplicateBecause: A Wedding Invitation is the nearest congratulations lesson, but that's accepting or declining an event by phone. This is a doorstep visit where the congratulations are the easy part and the real move is deciding not to be another guest — offering, leaving, doing the washing-up.

title: The Diagnosis
summary: Tell your best friend you're seriously ill.
whoElse: Tom, your oldest friend — he'll want to fix it, and he can't.
phrases: Sit down a minute. I've got something to tell you.
It's not good, I'm afraid.
I'm going to say it plainly, because I've practised it.
They found something. They're operating in March.
I don't know yet. That's the honest answer.
Please don't go and look it up tonight.
I don't want it to be the only thing we talk about.
If I don't want to talk about it, I'll say so — you're not treading on eggshells.
I'd rather you rang me about something stupid, actually.
Don't tell the others yet. Let me do it.
notDuplicateBecause: At the Doctor's is describing symptoms to a professional, and Bad News puts the student on the comforting side. Here the student is the one with the news, managing someone else's shock and setting terms for how they want to be treated afterwards.

title: Calling It a Day
summary: Tell your business partner you're retiring.
whoElse: Nadia, your partner of twenty years — she built half of it and isn't ready to stop.
phrases: I've been trying to find the right week to say this.
I'm going to stop at the end of the year.
It's not a decision I've come to lightly.
It's nothing to do with you, and I know that's what everyone says.
I've had enough. That's really all it is.
I'm not asking you to talk me out of it.
I'd like us to do this properly, over months, not weeks.
What would you want it to look like?
Whatever we agree, I'd rather agree it with you than with lawyers.
Take a week. Be cross with me if you want.
notDuplicateBecause: Resigning is leaving a boss for another job, with a counter-offer in the air; The Handover is the practical download. This is retirement — nowhere to go next, no better offer to blame, and an equal on the other side of the table who owns half of what you're walking away from.

title: Telling Your Mum
summary: Come out to your mother.
whoElse: Your mum, Eileen — she loves you, and she's about to say something clumsy.
phrases: There's something I want to tell you. It's nothing bad.
I've wanted to say this for a while.
I'm gay, Mum.
I'm not asking you to be alright with it today.
You can ask me anything. Genuinely.
I know that's not what you were expecting.
That's not really how it works, but I know what you mean.
I'd rather you asked than guessed.
Nothing's changed. I'm exactly who I was on Sunday.
Have a think, and ring me when you want. I'm not going anywhere.
notDuplicateBecause: The Apology is the only existing lesson where the student says something costly about themselves, but there the student is in the wrong and offering repair. Here the student has done nothing wrong and is absorbing a clumsy first reaction without punishing it — a completely different footing.

title: Twenty Years On
summary: Face the person who bullied you at school.
whoElse: Gary — friendly, warm, delighted to see you, and remembers none of it.
phrases: God, I wouldn't have recognised you.
You don't remember, do you?
No, it was — I mean it wasn't just messing about, though.
It went on for about two years, Gary.
I'm not looking for anything, I just wasn't going to stand here and pretend.
It's a long time ago. It still happened.
I'd honestly rather you didn't say "we were kids".
